edge_1127.relationship: Scott answers Eley and Nield that they want class 'as an effect of discourse but also as "a structural attribute of societies" as if those two were contradictory', and that insisting on class forecloses other political categories: her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (2000)
edge_1127.evidence_note: Body read in full for revision 1.152 (ILWCH 57, 2000, pp. 69–75; Cambridge PDF; data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-spread.md §6.3); the abstract read for 1.147 is confirmed verbatim. Eley and Nield's essay 'will surely become an indispensable assignment in introductory graduate courses because it is synthetic in many senses' (p. 69); they 'are willing to accommodate all manner of deviations from the materialist analyses … especially what some have dubbed "the linguistic turn"', so that one 'might have punned wildly and titled the Eley/Nield essay, "Assent to Discourse"' (p. 69); 'Patrick Joyce has been expelled from the fold and Kathleen Canning is now at its center' (p. 69); 'there's a tension between Eley and Nield's desires to update the old social history by detaching it from its materialist assumptions, on the one hand, and to keep writing narratives of worker political agency, on the other' (pp. 69–70); they talk of gender 'but no mention of sex, homo- or heterosexuality, and sexual difference' (p. 70); Rancière's 1983 essay is 'an important corrective to Eley and Nield' (pp. 70–71); 'They want to define class as an effect of discourse but also as "a structural attribute of societies" as if those two were contradictory. To posit them as contradictory is to misunderstand Foucault's ideas about discourse'; 'Structures come into being through discourse: Class is one way of naming, understanding, and organizing certain forms of social inequality' (p. 71); her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (p. 72). Eley and Nield's reply (pp. 81–86 read): 'we have some problems with Scott's ungenerous critique … It is either discourse (here signified by Jacques Rancière and Michel Foucault) or materialist social history' (p. 83), while they 'wholeheartedly applaud Scott's citation of Rancière' (p. 84). Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay) and from languages_of_class → social, which carries the debate's bearing on the field. Earlier note (1.147): Publisher abstract only (ILWCH 57, 2000, 69–75); the article body is unread. Eley and Nield's essay is marked by a tension between detaching social history from "its materialist assumptions" and continuing "narratives of working-class political agency"; "By insisting that class is still the best way of analyzing inequality and mobilizing resistance to it, the authors foreclose other possibilities for thinking about contemporary politics and for writing critical history"; her questions "don't exclude class but they don't require it either". Moderate. Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay).
